rows.speaker: JJ, Q
rows.claim: The references to before sunrise and sunset denote the dawn and late-afternoon prayers.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The hours of night refer to the night prayer.
rows.anchor: in the hours of the night refers to the night prayer (ʿishāʾ; Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The day's ends refer to the midday and sunset prayers: midday closes the first part of the day and begins the second, while sunset closes the second part.
rows.anchor: the sunset prayer stands at the end of the second part of the day (Q)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Glorifying God at these times brings contentment with the reward God gives.
rows.anchor: one will be content with the reward that will be given by God (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase can mean becoming generally content with whatever God gives in worldly life.
rows.anchor: It can also mean that one will become generally content with whatever is given by God in the life of this world.

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Spiritually, seekers should be patient, devoted solely to their Master, turn from sin and concern with others' opinions, and persist in remembrance until selfhood vanishes in divine Presence and they witness the Beloved.
rows.anchor: they will become content in witnessing the Beloved (Aj)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: One dating view holds that the surah is Madinan except verses 52–55, which are Makkan.
rows.anchor: Some say it is Madinan except for vv. 52–55, which are Makkan (IK)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another dating view holds that the surah is Makkan except verses 19–22, which are Madinan.
rows.anchor: others say it is Makkan except for vv.19–22, which are from the Madinan period (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Most authorities regard the surah as containing both Makkan and Madinan verses.
rows.anchor: Most say it is a mix of Makkan and Madinan verses (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A tradition calls the surah remarkable because it came at night and by day, on journeys and at home, in war and peace, and includes abrogating and abrogated as well as clear and allegorical verses.
rows.anchor: and it has both muḥkam (unambiguous) and mutashābih (symbolic or allegorical) verses (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's name comes from its mention of pilgrimage in verse 27 and its wider treatment of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: takes its name from the mention of the ḥajj (pilgrimage) in v. 27 and also the broader discussion of it throughout.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening warns of the world's destruction and Resurrection, comparing them with the human life cycle.
rows.anchor: compared to the individual life cycle of human beings (vv.5–7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts the misguided and righteous through a garden parable and their respective afterlife reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: describing their reward or punishment in the Hereafter (vv.8–25)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pilgrimage rites begin with Abraham; their inward meaning is reverence reaching God, rather than sacrificial meat or other physical aspects.
rows.anchor:
lies in the inner state of reverence(
taqwā) that reaches God, not sacrificial meat or other physical aspects of the ḥajj

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators connect the rejection of prophets with the story of the cranes, known in the West as the Satanic Verses, especially in discussion of verse 52.
rows.anchor: some commentators have explained in terms of the “story of the cranes,” more popularly known in the West as the “Satanic Verses,”

rows.speaker: many scholars
rows.claim: Many scholars regard verses 39–41 as the first revelation permitting the Muslim community to use force in self-defense against persecution.
rows.anchor: many scholars to be the first verses revealed giving the Muslim community permission to resort to the use of force

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah includes significant treatments of Islam's relation to other religions and the Muslim community's place in history.
rows.anchor: the relationship of Islam to other religions and the place of the Muslim community in history (vv. 17, 34, 67, 78)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “Upon a brink” can mean worshipping in a state of doubt.
rows.anchor: “in a state of doubt” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The phrase can describe superficial belief located at the edge of consciousness rather than in the heart.
rows.anchor: one’s belief is superficial, on the outer reaches of one’s consciousness and not in the heart (R)

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī applies the verse to opportunistic Bedouins in the Prophet's time: they embraced Islam for material gain, affirmed him when wealthy with sons, then reverted when hardship and daughters came.
rows.anchor: According to al-Ṭabarī, this refers to people like the Bedouin of the Prophet’s time

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Others read the verse as a general description of hypocrites whose religion serves their superficial self-interest.
rows.anchor: For others this verse provides a general description of hypocrites, whose religion is informed by a superficial notion of what is good for them (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Those on the brink are toppled from faith by the slightest discomfort.
rows.anchor: They are upon a brink in that the slightest discomfort topples them from faith (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: They lose this world when expected material goods fail to arrive and lose the Hereafter through neglect of faith's true nature and rewards.
rows.anchor: and the Hereafter—because they were heedless of the true nature and rewards of faith (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When a man complained that his new religion had brought him no good, the Prophet replied that Islam is tested and refined like metals in fire.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “Islam is not something spoken. Islam melts, as fire melts away the impurities of iron, gold, and silver” (R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The surah is considered Makkan.
rows.anchor: from the Makkan period (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens by describing the virtues and righteous actions of believers.
rows.anchor: begins by describing the virtues and righteous actions of those who believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It recounts human development from clay through a blood clot to another creation, recalling 22:5.
rows.anchor: reminiscent of 22:5, recounts a human being’s development starting from a clot of blood and culminating in another creation (vv. 12–14)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recalling worldly blessings, the surah tells of Noah's struggle against his people's denial and rebuke and his journey in the ark.
rows.anchor: the sūrah narrates the story of Noah, his struggles with the denial and rebuke of his people, and his journey in the ark (vv. 23–41)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After brief mention of Moses and Jesus, the surah discusses humanity's tendency to divide into religious groups.
rows.anchor: Brief mention of Moses and Jesus follows, after which the sūrah dwells upon the human tendency to divide into religious groups (vv. 42–54)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's opponents voice reasons like Noah's people, and are reminded that Muhammad is no stranger to them.
rows.anchor: similar to those voiced by the people of Noah, and the Prophet’s people are reminded that he is no stranger to them (vv. 55–69)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposition of affluent and powerful people to prophets recurs throughout this surah, as elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: The opposition to prophets by the affluent and powerful is a recurrent theme in this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questions and answers about God's relation to creation form an uncommon linear argument against belief in multiple gods.
rows.anchor: provides a linear argument, a form uncommon in the Quran in general, against believing in multiple gods

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion warns that disbelievers facing their perdition will wish to return to do good instead of evil, but it will be too late.
rows.anchor: will desire to go back to the world in order to do good instead of evil, though it will be too late for them (vv.99–118)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grandeur of the Hereafter makes worldly life seem like a day or part of a day.
rows.anchor: will make their life in the world seem to them as a day or part of a day (v. 113)
